title: Invariants and monovariants
summary: For a process that repeats a move, find a quantity the move never changes (an invariant) or always changes in one direction (a monovariant). Invariants rule out end states; monovariants prove termination.
key_statements: \text{move } \Rightarrow\ \Phi(\text{state}) \text{ unchanged, or } \Phi \text{ strictly decreases in } \mathbb N
why: This is the olympiad form of conserved quantities in physics and of termination proofs in computer science.

title: Combinatorial games and strategies
summary: Two players alternate moves with full information. Positions split into winning and losing ones; strategy stealing, pairing strategies and the Sprague–Grundy theory of nim-values decide who wins.
why: Games are the cleanest place to practise quantifier alternation: a strategy is a proof object.

title: Generating functions and recurrences
summary: Encode a sequence as $\sum a_n x^n$; combinatorial constructions become algebraic operations, and recurrences become equations for the series.
why: They connect counting to analysis: singularities of the series give asymptotics, as in the Hardy–Ramanujan partition formula.

title: Graphs, trees and paths
summary: A graph is a set of vertices with edges between pairs. Degrees, paths, connectivity, trees (connected graphs with no cycles) and Euler tours are the basic notions.
key_statements: \text{tree on } n \text{ vertices} \iff \text{connected with } n-1 \text{ edges}
\text{Euler tour exists} \iff \text{connected and all degrees even}
why: Graphs model any pairwise relation, so most of combinatorics and much of computer science is written in this language.

timeline.title: The bridges of Königsberg
timeline.text: Shows no walk crosses each bridge once, the first theorem of graph theory.

title: Cycles, matchings and Hamiltonicity
summary: Hall's theorem characterises when a bipartite graph has a matching covering one side; Dirac's theorem gives a degree condition for a Hamiltonian cycle; Erdős–Gallai bounds edges without long cycles.
why: Matchings are the prototype of a min–max theorem; Hamiltonicity is the prototype of an NP-complete property.

timeline.title: Hall's marriage theorem
timeline.text: A bipartite graph has a matching saturating one side iff every subset has enough neighbours.

title: Graph colouring
summary: A proper colouring gives adjacent vertices different colours; $\chi(G)$ is the fewest colours needed. Brooks, the four colour theorem and Hadwiger's conjecture are the landmarks.
why: Colouring is scheduling and register allocation; chromatic number problems for geometric graphs are among the oldest open questions.

timeline.title: The four colour theorem
timeline.text: Every planar map can be coloured with four colours; the first major computer-assisted proof.

title: Extremal graph theory
summary: How many edges can a graph on $n$ vertices have without containing a fixed subgraph $H$? Turán answers it for cliques; Erdős–Stone for all non-bipartite $H$; bipartite $H$ remain largely open.
why: The bipartite case connects to Sidon sets and finite geometry, and is where algebraic constructions beat random ones.

timeline.title: Turán's theorem
timeline.text: The densest graph with no $K_{r+1}$ is the balanced complete $r$-partite graph.
